label: Convexity and Its Consequences
notes: Welcome to printed pages 175 through 183. The single hypothesis driving this chapter is that the metric of a CAT(0) space is convex. From that one inequality we will harvest unique geodesics, distance-non-increasing projections, contractibility, and the Bruhat-Tits fixed-point theorem. Stress that everything downstream is a consequence.

label: The Metric Is Convex
notes: State the central proposition: for any two geodesics the distance between corresponding points is a convex function of the parameter. Derive it from the CAT(0) comparison inequality applied to the Euclidean model, where the same statement is elementary. Emphasise that convexity is the engine, not a corollary.

label: Uniqueness of Geodesics
notes: Apply convexity to two geodesics sharing both endpoints. The distance between them is a convex function vanishing at both ends, hence identically zero. Conclude geodesics are unique and, by the same estimate, vary continuously with their endpoints. This is the first concrete payoff of the convex metric.

label: Convex Functions and Sets
notes: Define convex functions along geodesics and convex subsets as those containing the geodesic between any two of their points. Note that distance to a point and distance to a convex set are themselves convex functions. These definitions set up the projection theorem on the following slide.

label: Nearest-Point Projection
notes: State the projection theorem: onto a complete convex subset of a CAT(0) space there is a unique nearest point. Existence uses completeness and the convexity of the distance function; uniqueness uses the strict midpoint estimate. The projection map is the central construction of the chapter.

label: Projection Is a Retraction
notes: Show the projection does not increase distance. Compare the two segments from a pair of points to their projections using the convex quadrilateral estimate. Because the map fixes the convex set pointwise and is continuous, it is a retraction onto it. This non-expanding property is used repeatedly.

label: Convexity Between Geodesics
notes: Walk through the visual: two geodesics emanating into the space, with vertical segments measuring their separation at each parameter. The tops of those segments bow downward below the chord, the signature of convexity. Point out that the Euclidean comparison triangle is what licenses the inequality.

label: CAT(0) Spaces Are Contractible
notes: Use the geodesic retraction to a basepoint: slide every point along its unique geodesic to the centre. Continuity of geodesics in their endpoints makes this a genuine homotopy. Hence CAT(0) spaces are contractible, therefore aspherical, with all higher homotopy groups vanishing.

label: The Circumcenter
notes: Introduce the circumradius of a bounded set as the infimum of radii of enclosing balls. Convexity forces the centre realising it to be unique: two distinct centres would yield a strictly better midpoint centre. This circumcenter construction is canonical and isometry-equivariant.

label: Bruhat-Tits Fixed Point
notes: Combine uniqueness of the circumcenter with equivariance. A group acting by isometries with a bounded orbit fixes the circumcenter of that orbit, since isometries permute the orbit and hence fix its unique centre. This is the Bruhat-Tits fixed-point theorem, a cornerstone for actions on CAT(0) spaces.

label: Flat Subspaces
notes: Mention flat subspaces: isometrically embedded Euclidean pieces along which the convexity estimate becomes an equality. They mark where curvature is exactly zero and foreshadow the flat torus theorem. Tie this back to convexity being an inequality that flats saturate.

label: Synthesis and Takeaways
notes: Recap the dependency chain: convex metric implies unique geodesics, projections, contractibility, circumcenters, and fixed points. Encourage students to revisit the notebook's projection-and-center computation, where a point cloud is projected to a segment and the circumradius shrinks. One inequality organises the whole chapter.
